questions.question: Which command searches all **tracked** files for `TODO`, skipping `node_modules/` and other ignored files?
questions.explanation: `git grep` only looks at files Git tracks, so it's fast and skips build output. `-n` adds line numbers, and you can search an older version: `git grep TODO v1.0`.

questions.question: Which command lists every file Git is tracking?
questions.explanation: `git ls-files` prints tracked paths, one per line. `git ls-files --others --exclude-standard` lists untracked files that aren't ignored, and `git ls-files -i --exclude-standard -c` tracked files that match an ignore rule.

questions.question: You want a script to run the linter automatically before every commit, and block the commit if it fails. Where does Git look for it?
questions.explanation: If `pre-commit` exits with a non-zero code, the commit is aborted. Other hooks include `commit-msg` and `pre-push`. `.git/hooks` isn't committed, so teams share hooks with a tool like the `pre-commit` framework, or with `git config core.hooksPath .githooks`. `git commit --no-verify` skips them.

questions.question: You cloned a project that uses submodules, and the `vendor/lib` folder is empty. Which command fills it?
questions.explanation: A submodule is another repository pinned at a specific commit inside yours. A normal clone only creates the empty folder. Next time, clone with `git clone --recurse-submodules <url>` to do both in one step.

questions.question: Your repository needs large binary files (videos, PSDs, trained models) and clones are getting very slow. Which tool is built for this?
questions.explanation: Git LFS (Large File Storage) stores small pointer files in Git and keeps the real content on a separate server, downloading only the versions you check out. `git lfs track` writes a rule to `.gitattributes`, which you commit. Every version of a big file stored in normal Git stays in every clone forever.

questions.question: In a huge monorepo you only work in `services/billing`. Which feature lets you check out just that folder?
questions.explanation: Sparse checkout limits which folders appear in your working tree, while the history stays complete. Combine it with a partial clone (`git clone --filter=blob:none --sparse <url>`) to also avoid downloading the other files' contents.

questions.question: You need a zip of the project as it was at `v1.2.0`, without the `.git` folder. Which command?
questions.explanation: `git archive` packs a tree from any commit or tag, containing only tracked files. Files can be left out with `export-ignore` in `.gitattributes`. `git bundle` is different: it packs commits and history into a file you can clone from offline.

questions.question: How do you prove that a commit really came from you, not from someone who just set `user.name` to your name?
options: Sign it with a GPG or SSH key: `git commit -S`
questions.explanation: Anyone can set any name and email, so `-S` adds a cryptographic signature that GitHub shows as "Verified". Turn it on everywhere with `git config --global commit.gpgsign true`. Lowercase `-s` only adds a `Signed-off-by` text line, a declaration used by some projects, not a signature.

questions.question: A 2 GB `data.csv` was committed a year ago and deleted later, but every clone still downloads it. Which tool removes it from the entire history?
options: `git revert` on the commit that added it
questions.explanation: `git filter-repo` (a separate install, recommended over the old `git filter-branch`) rewrites every commit without that file. All hashes change, so you must force-push and everyone must re-clone. `git rm` and `git revert` only add new commits; the file stays in the old ones.

questions.question: A big "reformat all code" commit now shows up as the last change on every line in `git blame`. How do you make blame look past it?
options: List its hash in `.git-blame-ignore-revs` and run `git config blame.ignoreRevsFile .git-blame-ignore-revs`
Use `git blame --since` with the date before the commit
questions.explanation: Blame then attributes those lines to the commit before the reformat. For a one-off, use `git blame --ignore-rev <hash> file`. GitHub's blame view also reads a `.git-blame-ignore-revs` file in the repository root.

questions.question: Commands in a large repository have become slow. Which command sets up background jobs that keep the repository optimised?
questions.explanation: `git maintenance start` registers the repository and schedules regular tasks (prefetching, packing, commit-graph updates). `git gc` does a one-off cleanup. `git fsck` only checks the repository's integrity.

questions.question: Why did Git 2.23 add `git switch` and `git restore`?
options: To split the overloaded `git checkout`: `switch` changes branches, `restore` restores files
Because `git checkout` was removed from Git
They are faster versions that skip the staging area
questions.explanation: `git checkout` does both jobs, so a typo can discard your edits when you meant to change branch. `git checkout` still works and appears in many tutorials: `checkout -b` ≈ `switch -c`, and `checkout -- file` ≈ `restore file`.
